issues.issue: The reply took 62.518 seconds against the 30-second limit.

The reply said “Stock for the teapot set is currently 3, so it may be fulfilled once stock is allocated.” The count came from turn 1. Turn 3 only looked up the order and returned “waiting for stock.” The records support the order status and the earlier stock count. They do not establish current stock at turn 3 or how it would be allocated.

Rule 3 says a reservation holds the requested quantity “and no more.” The client sends the same reservation twice using `range(2)`, even after a successful response. With enough stock for both requests, the service subtracts the quantity and appends a reservation each time. This follows from the code. The test made no reservation.

## Notes

The seal was intact. The audit recorded no changes to the three exchanges, and the findings file listed no findings. The expected stock checks, stock backend calls, order lookup and direct OpenAI calls appear in the trace.

The stock replies matched the backend counts of 3 teapot sets and 12 blue mugs. The order status matched the lookup. The session output totals were 82, 142 and 132 tokens against a 2,000-token limit. Turns 1 and 3 took 4.376 and 4.219 seconds.

In turn 2, the case-note and department calls each took about 25 seconds in the model API record. The app waits for both before returning the reply (`app.py:117`–`119`). The records show the time spent waiting and leave the cause of the upstream delay unresolved.

I checked the application code and read `state.json` and `stock.json`. The workspace files showed order 6210 as “waiting for stock,” three case notes, and stock counts matching the recorded lookups. There was no sealed app-state snapshot. The lookup uses the order number alone (`app.py:54`), and the records do not establish who owns order 6210. The test did not exercise another customer's order, refunds, or reservations.
